settings.heading: Learn More
settings.intro:
World in Common is a starting point, not a complete theory. This page collects books, organisations, tools, and projects that have influenced the questions we ask.

We do not agree with everything any author or organisation says. These are invitations to explore, not approved doctrines.

settings.heading: Start here
settings.text:
The Man Who Quit Money — Mark Sundeen

The first book we recommend.

This book follows Daniel Suelo, who stopped using money and lived through foraging, sharing, volunteering, reuse, and community. It raises a question that sits close to the centre of World in Common:

How much of our relationship with money is necessary—and how much have we simply accepted by default?

The book is not a simple instruction to abandon money. Its more useful contribution is the tension between individual freedom, community, responsibility, and the practical difficulty of living differently.

Our own position is different from Suelo’s. We are interested in the question without pretending that everyone should live in a cave or reject all exchange. We are interested in building alternatives that let people participate in society without being completely controlled by its dominant systems.

settings.heading: Monetary systems and equality
settings.text:
• Human Rights Foundation — Financial Freedom — education and grants supporting financial tools for activists and civil society.
  • Progressive Bitcoiner — resources exploring Bitcoin through social justice and human-rights perspectives.
  • BTC Map — an open map of places that accept Bitcoin, built on OpenStreetMap data.
  • Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System — the original Bitcoin white paper.
  • Banco de Portugal — Cryptoassets — official Portuguese information and warnings.
  • Autoridade Tributária — Cryptoassets — official Portuguese tax information. Search for “Criptoativos”.

settings.heading: Community and alternative ways of living
settings.text:
• Foundation for Intentional Community — communities, co-living, cohousing, ecovillages, and resources for starting or joining intentional communities.
  • Global Ecovillage Network — a global network connecting regenerative communities and initiatives.
  • Shareable — practical ideas about sharing, co-ops, platform co-operativism, and community ownership.
  • Community Land Trust Network — models for protecting land and housing from pure speculation.

settings.heading: Open source and shared tools
settings.text:
• Open Source Initiative — what “open source” legally means and how approved licences work.
  • Software Freedom Conservancy — supporting ethical technology, software freedom, copyleft, and the right to repair, improve, and reinstall software.
  • Codeberg — a community-oriented home for open-source software projects.
  • Free Software Foundation — software freedom, user rights, and the GNU project.

settings.heading: Books to explore next
settings.text:
Money, debt, and economic systems

  • Debt: The First 5,000 Years — David Graeber
  • The Dawn of Everything — David Graeber and David Wengrow
  • Small Is Beautiful — E. F. Schumacher
  • The Price of Tomorrow — Jeff Booth
  • The Creature from Jekyll Island — G. Edward Griffin — read critically; useful for understanding one influential critique of central banking, but not a neutral account.

Community and alternative living

  • The Good Life — Helen and Scott Nearing
  • Deep Economy — Bill McKibben
  • How to Build a Regenerative Village
  • The Art of Gathering — Priya Parker
  • Emergent Strategy — adrienne maree brown

Technology, power, and open source

  • Free Software, Free Society — Richard M. Stallman — important, but read critically and separately from the person.
  • The Cathedral and the Bazaar — Eric S. Raymond
  • The Age of Surveillance Capitalism — Shoshana Zuboff
  • The Master Switch — Tim Wu

Fiction and imagination

  • The Dispossessed — Ursula K. Le Guin
  • Parable of the Sower — Octavia E. Butler
  • Always Coming Home — Ursula K. Le Guin

settings.heading: A note on recommendations
settings.text:
Some links may eventually become affiliate links. If that happens, we will label them clearly. We will not pretend that an affiliate recommendation is independent.

We also distinguish between:

  • ideas we find useful
  • organisations we respect
  • claims we have verified
  • claims we are still investigating

The point of this page is not to create a canon. It is to make the path visible so other people can explore, disagree, and add better sources.

settings.heading: Still learning
settings.text:
I am always learning, and this project is not built around the idea that I already have all the answers.

If you have read a book, article, essay, research paper, or watched something that you think belongs in these conversations, send it to me. I will publish my reading list and keep adding to it as I explore new ideas.

You can also tell me:

  • what I should read next
  • what you think I have misunderstood
  • what subjects I should explore
  • what communities or projects I should know about
  • what solutions are already working somewhere else

You do not have to agree with the project to contribute to it. Teach me something new, challenge an assumption, or point me toward a perspective I have missed.

settings.heading: Contribute
settings.text:
World in Common is built in public. You do not need to be part of an organisation, have a platform, or agree with every idea here to contribute.

World in Common is not meant to be one person broadcasting a finished worldview. It is an attempt to build a better understanding in public, with other people.
